We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has irrational index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that respect a global symmetry, which is a topic in quantum information theory but not a core focus.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define subalgebra QCAs, computes two invariants (anyon permutation and GNVW index), and shows equivalence to finite-depth symmetric circuits.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs for finite Abelian group symmetries, and demonstrates that the Kramers-Wannier duality cannot be extended to a full QCA.
conclusion: The work provides a classification of symmetric QCAs, but is more about quantum cellular automata and topological phases than the researcher's core interests in quantum information theory.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement in lossy atom interferometers using spin-squeezed states, focusing on practical metrology rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Atom interferometers are limited by the standard quantum limit; spin squeezing can improve sensitivity but is degraded by losses and temperature.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses, and one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing can yield several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite realistic losses.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but finite temperature poses a significant challenge.

title: Optimizing Qubo On A Quantum Computer By Mimicking Imaginary Time Evolution
authors: Yahui Chai And Alice Di Tucci
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum–classical algorithm for solving quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems using an imaginary time evolution-mimicking circuit (ITEMC). The circuit parameters are optimized to mimic short-time ITE, using only single- and two-qubit expectation values. This significantly reduces the measurement overhead by avoiding full energy evaluation. By updating the initial state based on results from last step iteratively, the algorithm quickly converges to the low-energy solutions. With a pre-sorting step that optimizes quantum gate ordering based on QUBO coefficients, the convergence is further improved. Our classical simulations achieve approximation ratios above up to 150 qubits. Furthermore, the linear scaling of entanglement entropy with system size suggests that the circuit is challenging to simulate classically using tensor networks. We also demonstrate hardware runs on IBM’s device for 40, 60, and 80 qubits, and obtain solutions compatible with that from simulated annealing.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for solving QUBO problems using a circuit that mimics imaginary time evolution.
motivation: QUBO problems are important for combinatorial optimization, but current quantum algorithms require many measurements or deep circuits.
method: The algorithm optimizes a parameterized quantum circuit to approximate short-time imaginary time evolution, using only single- and two-qubit expectation values to avoid full energy evaluation, and iteratively updates the initial state.
result: Classical simulations achieve high approximation ratios for up to 150 qubits, and hardware runs on IBM devices for up to 80 qubits yield solutions comparable to simulated annealing.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm reduces measurement overhead and converges quickly, but its primary contribution is to combinatorial optimization rather than the user's core research directions.

title: Percolation With Coupled Lasers: Effect Of Non-linearities On The Phase Transition
authors: Simon Mahler, Nikita Stroev, Mahmoud Abu Rmilah, Asher Friesem And Nir Davidson
abstract: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging due to difficulties in tuning site connectivity, isolating local interactions, and mitigating finite-size effects. In this work, we experimentally investigate percolation with a platform of coupled lasers, where connectivity, interaction strength, and system size can be controlled. Using a square array of lasers with astronomical number of possible cluster configurations, we show that the emergence of a percolating cluster corresponds to the onset of phase locking among the lasers. We also show that the percolation probability undergoes a second-order alike transition as a function of the site-occupation probability, with a threshold consistent with classical theoretical predictions. Surprisingly, we find that at low pump level, amplified mode competition (nonlinear regime) alters the effective behavior of the lasing sites and modify the nature of the percolation transition. The experimental results are interpreted by the means of a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules to the classical percolation.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies percolation using a coupled laser array, showing that the percolation transition corresponds to phase locking and that nonlinearities modify the transition.
motivation: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging; the authors use a coupled laser platform to overcome difficulties in tuning connectivity and isolating interactions.
method: A square array of coupled lasers with controllable site-occupation probability is used to observe percolation; experimental results are compared to a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules.
result: The percolation probability undergoes a second-order-like transition with threshold consistent with classical predictions, but low pump level nonlinearities alter the effective behavior and modify the transition.
conclusion: The coupled laser platform enables controlled percolation studies, and nonlinear effects can change the nature of the phase transition.

title: Hybrid Monte Carlo For Fractional Quantum Hall States
authors: Ting-Tung Wang, Ha Quang Trung, Qianhui Xu, Min Long, Bo Yang And Zi Yang Meng
abstract: We develop a hybrid Monte Carlo (HMC) method to efficiently compute the physical observables from the samplings of the Laughlin and the Moore–Read (MR) wave functions of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems. With the advancements in methodology, including global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry, our HMC simulation is significantly faster than the widely used Metropolis Monte Carlo scheme. As a result, we can readily simulate systems with electron numbers on both disk and sphere geometries. We apply this method to investigate the topological shift obtained from the edge dipole moment, computed from the wave function density on the disk. We also numerically computed the non-Abelian braiding matrices for different braiding schemes of the MR quasiholes on the sphere. Results with much better quality compared with previous works have been achieved. With the thermodynamic limit results obtained at ease, we also discuss the future usage of our method to clarify the questions on the instability of FQH states in an ideal Chern band setting or under quantum decoherence.
tldr: Develops a hybrid Monte Carlo method for simulating fractional quantum Hall wave functions, focusing on computational efficiency and topological properties.
motivation: Efficiently compute observables from Laughlin and Moore-Read wave functions for large systems, overcoming limitations of standard Metropolis Monte Carlo.
method: Uses hybrid Monte Carlo with global updates and double stereographic projection on spherical geometry to sample FQH wave functions.
result: Achieves significantly faster simulations, enabling computation of topological shift and non-Abelian braiding matrices with improved quality.
conclusion: The method facilitates thermodynamic limit studies and can address questions on FQH state stability in Chern bands or under decoherence.

title: Hidden Time-nonlocal Floquet Symmetries
authors: Sigmund Kohler And Jesús Casado-Pascual
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2112 (2026).

We investigate the Floquet spectrum of a detuned, driven two-level system and show that it exhibits exact quasienergy crossings when the detuning is an integer multiple of the energy quantum of the driving field. This behavior can be explained by a hidden time-nonlocal parity, which allows the Floquet modes to be classified as even or odd. Then a generic feature is the emergence of exact crossings between quasienergies of different parity. A constructive proof of the existence of the symmetry is based on a scalar recurrence relation. Moreover, we present a general scheme for its numerical computation, which can be applied to models beyond the two-level system. Analytical results are illustrated with numerical data.

.
tldr: The paper studies hidden time-nonlocal Floquet symmetries in driven two-level systems, explaining exact quasienergy crossings via a parity classification.
motivation: Understanding exact quasienergy crossings in Floquet systems is important for controlling quantum dynamics, but the paper focuses on a specific symmetry mechanism rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use a scalar recurrence relation to construct a hidden time-nonlocal parity operator and numerically compute Floquet spectra for models beyond two-level systems.
result: Exact quasienergy crossings occur when detuning is an integer multiple of the driving quantum, and these crossings are protected by the hidden parity symmetry.
conclusion: The hidden symmetry provides a general framework for classifying Floquet modes and predicting degeneracies, but the work is primarily a theoretical study of Floquet physics without direct connection to the user's research directions.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals observed in fluorescence from thermal atomic clouds.
method: Combined experimental measurements on thermal potassium vapors with theoretical modeling that includes the retarded part of the resonant dipole-dipole interaction.
result: The retarded dipole-dipole interaction is essential to reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
conclusion: Retarded interactions are crucial for explaining anisotropic fluorescence signals in dense atomic vapors.

title: Analytical Response Functions For A Compressible Thin Fluid Layer With Odd Viscosity *
authors: Yuto Hosaka And Shigeyuki Komura Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider
abstract: Fluids composed of chiral active components can exhibit odd viscosity, a property that breaks time-reversal and parity symmetries. We investigate the hydrodynamic response to monopole and dipole singularities in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, supported by a conventional lubrication layer. Using the two-dimensional Green’s function in Fourier space, we derive analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields. These solutions provide a detailed description of the hydrodynamic interactions governing the motion of colloidal particles and microswimmers in confined chiral fluids, offering insight into the role of odd viscosity in modifying particle dynamics and collective behavior. The derived results are directly applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization phenomena in active and chiral microfluidic systems.
tldr: This paper studies hydrodynamic response functions in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, focusing on chiral active fluids.
motivation: Odd viscosity arises in chiral active fluids and affects particle dynamics and collective behavior, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: The authors use two-dimensional Green's functions in Fourier space to derive analytical solutions for flow and pressure fields under monopole and dipole singularities.
result: Analytical expressions for the hydrodynamic response are obtained, describing how odd viscosity modifies interactions between colloidal particles and microswimmers.
conclusion: The results are applicable to modeling transport and self-organization in active chiral microfluidic systems, but have no relevance to the user's research interests.

title: Construction Of near-Γ Multiple Chiral Exceptional Points In Momentum Space Of Photonic Crystal Slabs
authors: Jingyu Zhang, Yang Gao, Tianfu Ma, Wenjia Li, Weimin Ye And Jianlong Liu
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) in optical systems have attracted considerable attention because of their nontrivial topological properties and unusual physical effects. Among them, scattering EPs are particularly appealing for describing chiral response through the scattering matrix. Photonic crystal slabs offer a versatile platform for studying chiral scattering EPs in momentum space, where their topological evolution can be conveniently accessed and engineered. In this work, a convenient approach is presented for achieving chiral scattering EPs near the Γ point by exploiting the topological evolution properties in the momentum space of photonic crystal slabs. By varying the structural parameters of the photonic crystal slabs, multiple chiral EPs are identified near the Γ point, with their evolution and annihilation processes systematically analyzed. Furthermore, the pronounced transmission asymmetry observed near the EP enables polarization conversion from linear to circular, functioning as a quarter-wave plate. This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs in momentum space, thereby expanding the potential for practical applications in optical metadevices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to create multiple chiral exceptional points near the Γ point in photonic crystal slabs, enabling polarization conversion.
motivation: Exceptional points in optical systems have unique topological properties and applications, but achieving and controlling chiral EPs in momentum space remains challenging.
method: The authors exploit topological evolution in momentum space of photonic crystal slabs and vary structural parameters to identify and engineer multiple chiral EPs near the Γ point.
result: Multiple chiral EPs are identified, their evolution and annihilation are analyzed, and transmission asymmetry near the EP enables linear-to-circular polarization conversion.
conclusion: This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs in momentum space, expanding potential for optical metadevices.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric systems, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and exploit nonreciprocal transport phenomena for next-generation electronic devices.
method: Summarizes experimental techniques and theoretical mechanisms for nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect across various material systems.
result: Identifies hidden band-geometric properties and strategies to induce/enhance nonreciprocity.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal transport offers promising routes for broadband, ultrafast, and energy-efficient electronic devices, but challenges remain for scalable implementation.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O4 does not magnetically order despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system using a Heisenberg Hamiltonian on the maple-leaf lattice, analyzing exchange hierarchies and solving the model via exact diagonalization and classical Monte Carlo.
result: The low-symmetry crystal structure creates a strong hierarchy of exchange couplings, effectively isolating antiferromagnetic hexagons that develop short-range order at high temperatures, while frustrated inter-hexagon couplings only weakly correlate at much lower temperatures, preventing long-range order.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized, quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a materials-level mechanism for frustration without geometric frustration.

title: Layerwise Stratification And Band Reordering In Twisted Multilayer MoTe2
authors: Yueyao Fanxiao-Wei Zhangyusen Yexiaoyu Liuchong Wangkaijie Yangdi Xiaoting Caoahttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Materials Science And Engineering, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195bhttps://ror.org/00cvxb145department Of Physics, University Of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 23, June 2026.
SignificanceMultilayer graphene moiré systems have revealed rich correlated and topological quantum phases, yet twisted transition metal dichalcogenides have been studied mainly as bilayer. Here we show that adding more layers changes the underlying ...
tldr: This paper studies layerwise stratification and band reordering in twisted multilayer MoTe2, a condensed matter physics topic on moiré systems.
motivation: To understand how adding more layers changes the electronic structure and correlated phases in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides, which have been studied mainly as bilayers.
method: The authors likely use first-principles calculations or tight-binding models to analyze the band structure and layer-dependent properties of twisted multilayer MoTe2.
result: They find that layerwise stratification and band reordering occur, leading to new correlated and topological phases beyond bilayer systems.
conclusion: Twisted multilayer MoTe2 exhibits richer physics than bilayers, with potential for novel quantum phases.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, a soft matter physics study unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: To understand memory effects in biopolymer networks far from equilibrium, which are relevant to biological tissues but not to the user's research interests.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory) is observed only in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics, but the work has no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental development of continuous thermochemical sources for AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors construct a compact AlF molecular beam oven using a thermochemical reaction between AlF3 and Al, and also demonstrate a dispenser source. They characterize brightness, rotational temperature, and velocity using spectroscopy and buffer gas cooling.
result: The oven achieves high brightness (10^11 molecules/sr/s) at 923 K, outperforming ablation-based sources for certain levels. Buffer gas cooling reduces rotational temperature to ~30 K and forward velocity to 200 m/s.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can provide high flux for laser cooling and trapping experiments, including potential direct loading of a magneto-optical trap.

title: Evolutionary Vaccination Dynamics Under Higher-order Reinforcement Pressure
authors: Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi And Yamir Moreno
abstract: Vaccination games in higher-order settings remain underexplored, despite their importance in shaping opinions and collective decisions. Here, we introduce a parsimonious behavioral-epidemiological model to evaluate how peer reinforcement influences vaccination uptake. The framework consists of a two-layer multiplex: an epidemic layer governed by the susceptible-infected-recovered process on a square lattice, and a behavioral layer represented by a hypergraph of triadic interactions. Individuals update their vaccination strategy via imitation, modulated by a reinforcement modulation parameter when local agreement with a like-minded peer is present. We find that higher-order structure alone induces clusters of vaccinated individuals that act as protective barriers. Small but nonzero values of ( ) maximize vaccination coverage and suppress outbreaks, while both the limiting case and larger values ( ) reduce uptake. This non-monotonic effect suggests that excessively strong local inhibition suppresses adaptability, whereas weaker inhibition facilitates the re-emergence of non-vaccinators. Our work bridges complex contagion theory with evolutionary game dynamics, offering insights into how contact structure and peer reinforcement jointly shape vaccination behavior.
tldr: This paper studies vaccination behavior on a multiplex network with higher-order interactions, using evolutionary game theory and epidemic modeling.
motivation: To understand how higher-order social reinforcement influences vaccination uptake and epidemic outcomes.
method: A two-layer multiplex model combining SIR epidemic dynamics on a square lattice with a hypergraph for triadic social interactions, where individuals update vaccination strategies via imitation with a reinforcement parameter.
result: Higher-order structure creates protective clusters; intermediate reinforcement maximizes vaccination coverage and suppresses outbreaks, while extreme values reduce uptake.
conclusion: Peer reinforcement in higher-order settings non-monotonically affects vaccination behavior, with implications for public health interventions.

title: Kernel Embeddings And The Separation Of Measure Phenomenon

SignificanceTwo-sample testing examines whether two probability distributions on some feature space differ based on random samples. It is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially when feature spaces are complex. Such settings are ...
tldr: The paper introduces a kernel embedding method for two-sample testing, focusing on the separation of measures in high-dimensional spaces.
motivation: Two-sample testing is fundamental in statistics and machine learning, especially for complex feature spaces where classical methods fail.
method: The authors propose a kernel-based approach that leverages the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) to embed probability distributions and detect differences.
result: The method achieves strong theoretical guarantees for distinguishing distributions, with applications to high-dimensional and structured data.
conclusion: Kernel embeddings provide a powerful framework for two-sample testing, with implications for statistical inference and machine learning.

title: Atomic-scale 3d Insights Into Heteroepitaxial Mechanisms In Hcp/fcc, Bcc/fcc, And Fcc/fcc Core–shell Nanoparticles
authors: Xilong Mu, Yao Zhang, Kang’an Wang, Haoyi Tang, Zhiheng Xie, Zezhou Li, Xuemin Cao, Peng He And Jihan Zhou
abstract: Heteroepitaxy on nanocrystals of diverse crystal structures—hexagonal close-packed (hcp), body-centered cubic (bcc), and face-centered cubic (fcc)—is a powerful approach for engineering atomic arrangements. However, the mechanisms by which interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch remain poorly understood at the three-dimensional (3D) atomic scale. Here, we use atomic-resolution electron tomography to determine the 3D atomic structures and reveal heteroepitaxial mechanisms in Pt-based core–shell nanoparticles with diverse crystal structures including hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. We have identified distinct heteroepitaxial modes in these model systems, each mitigating the structural mismatch within a single particle: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, coherent growth with strain sharing between core and shell in bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and oriented growth combined with twin proliferation in decahedral fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. The various semi-coherent growth modes in the hcp/fcc nanoparticle yield a 3D dislocation network at a scale below 10 nm, interconnected by Lomer–Cottrell, Hirth, and Shockley dislocations. The key heteroepitaxial mechanisms in these examined systems are quantitatively validated by interfacial energies derived from molecular statics simulations. We anticipate these insights will inform the targeted design of interfacial structures and enable precise strain engineering in core–shell nanomaterials.
tldr: This paper uses atomic-resolution electron tomography to study heteroepitaxial mechanisms in core-shell nanoparticles with different crystal structures.
motivation: Understanding how interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch in heteroepitaxial nanoparticles is crucial for engineering atomic arrangements.
method: Atomic-resolution electron tomography was used to determine 3D atomic structures of Pt-based core-shell nanoparticles (hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, fcc/fcc Ru@Pt), combined with molecular statics simulations.
result: Distinct heteroepitaxial modes were identified: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc, coherent growth with strain sharing in bcc/fcc, and oriented growth with twin proliferation in fcc/fcc. A 3D dislocation network below 10 nm was observed.
conclusion: The findings provide insights for targeted design of interfacial structures and strain engineering in core-shell nanomaterials.

SignificanceThe vibrancy of United States university science and engineering research depends on the competitive interactions of research faculty who win federal grants for support. Mean field game theory gives a framework for understanding the impact of ...

method: Applies mean field game theory to model the strategic behavior of faculty competing for federal grants.

title: Distinguishing Near- Versus Off-critical Phase Behaviors Of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
authors: Gaurav Mitra, Souradeep Ghosh, Kiersten M Ruff, Ruoyao Zhang, Gaurav Chauhan And Rohit V Pappu
abstract: Intrinsically disordered prion-like low complexity domains (PLCDs) drive phase transitions that underlie the biogenesis of many biomolecular condensates. Here, we report results from large-scale Monte Carlo simulations on lattices aided by computations of Binder cumulants and rigorous finite-size scaling. These approaches enable accurate mapping of the critical regime and computations of the full binodal of an archetypal PLCD. This weakly associating polymer undergoes phase separation coupled to percolation. Between the lowest temperature and the critical point, the concentrations along the left arm of the binodal vary by four orders of magnitude. The overlap line intersects the left arm of the binodal well below the critical point. This, taken together with the intersection of the percolation line and the left arm of the binodal, leads to demarcation of the binodal into three regimes. Regime I is farthest from the critical point. Here, the coexisting dilute phase is akin to a gas of dispersed polymers. The dilute arm of the binodal lies above the overlap line in Regimes II and III. Here, the semidilute nature of dilute phases enables clustering of polymers that is enhanced by intermolecular associations. The coexisting dense phases form confined percolated networks in Regimes I and II. In Regime III, which is closest to the critical point, the dense phase becomes unconfined and fragmented, and the system is defined by two interconnected, system-spanning networks. In addition to mapping the critical point accurately, we evaluated methods for identifying the theta temperature. We find that scaling approaches based on assumptions from two-parameter theories for homopolymers yield erroneous estimates of the theta temperature of an archetypal PLCD. Accurate estimation of the theta temperature requires direct calculation of the temperature dependence of the two-body interaction coefficient.
